facts: Home to the Andromeda Galaxy, the most distant thing visible to the naked eye at 2.5 million light-years.
The princess of the myth — chained to a rock as a sacrifice before Perseus rescued her.
Its brightest star, Alpheratz, technically belongs to the Square of Pegasus.
One of 14 constellations invented by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s.
Named after the air pump, an 18th-century scientific instrument.
Contains the planetary nebula NGC 3132, nicknamed the Eight-Burst Nebula.
Named after the spectacular birds of paradise New Guinea explorers brought back to Europe.
Created by Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman around 1600.
One of the southern constellations invisible from most of the USA.
The water-bearer of the zodiac, associated with floods and the rainy season.
Its Eta Aquarid meteor shower comes from debris of Halley's Comet.
The great globular cluster M2 floats here, 40,000 light-years away.
Contains the Eagle Nebula, home of the famous Pillars of Creation.
The star Altair anchors the Summer Triangle and spins once every 9 hours, fast enough to visibly flatten it.
In mythology it was Zeus's eagle, bearer of his thunderbolts.
The celestial altar of the gods, on which they swore oaths before battling the Titans.
Lies in the Milky Way near the galactic center, rich in star clusters.
One of the 48 classical constellations of Ptolemy, still official today.
The golden-fleeced ram of the Argonaut legend.
Its brightest star, Hamal, means 'the head of the ram' in Arabic.
The First Point of Aries, the zero mark of right ascension, sat here in antiquity — precession has since carried it into the Fishes.
Usually drawn as a man carrying a goat on his shoulder — Capella, the 'Goat Star'.
Capella is actually four stars: two giants and two red dwarfs.
Holds Menkalinan, a famous eclipsing binary of changing brightness.
Shaped like a kite chasing the Great Bear around the pole.
Arcturus, its anchor star, is the brightest star north of the celestial equator.
Arcturus's light opened the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, having left the star in 1893 — the year of the previous fair.
The engraver's tool, invented by Lacaille to honor the draughtsman's craft.
Split from the larger figure of the Ship long ago.
One of the faintest of the 88 constellations.
Camelopardalis, the giraffe — a faint patch of sky with no stars brighter than 4th magnitude.
Named by Petrus Plancius in 1613, replacing an older 'Camel' figure.
Contains NGC 2403, one of the brightest galaxies outside the Messier list.
Cancer, the crab sent by Hera to nip Hercules — it was crushed, then immortalized in the sky.
Contains the Beehive Cluster, visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch since antiquity.
The Tropic of Cancer got its name because the Sun passed through this constellation at the June solstice.
Canes Venatici, added by Hevelius in 1687 from stars once assigned to the Great Bear.
Holds M51, the Whirlpool Galaxy — the first galaxy recognized as a spiral.
Cor Caroli, 'Charles's Heart', honors King Charles I of England.
Home of Sirius, the brightest star in the entire night sky.
Sirius has a companion, Sirius B, the first white dwarf ever found — 'the Pup'.
Contains the rich open cluster M41, just south of Sirius.
Procyon, its brightest star, means 'before the dog' — it rises just ahead of Sirius.
One of the smallest constellations on the official 88 list.
Procyon is also one of the nearest star systems, at just 11.5 light-years.
The sea-goat: part goat, part fish, in myth the god Pan taking refuge in a river.
Its Deneb Algedi ('tail of the goat') is an eclipsing binary.
The Winter Solstice point lies in Capricorn — the Tropic of Capricorn is named for it.
Carina, the keel of the great ship Argo, split into four pieces in 1930.
Holds Canopus, the second-brightest star in the sky.
The erratic hypergiant Eta Carinae may one day light up as a supernova visible in daylight.
Its W shape makes it one of the easiest constellations to find.
It holds Cassiopeia A, one of the strongest radio sources in the sky.
Tycho's Star, a supernova seen in 1572, flared up here and helped overturn Aristotle's 'unchanging heavens'.
Alpha Centauri is the closest star system to Earth — just 4.4 light-years away.
Holds Omega Centauri, the grandest globular cluster visible from the Northern Hemisphere's edge.
In myth, this was Chiron, the wise tutor of heroes.
The king beside Cassiopeia — a dim figure shaped like a child's house drawing.
Delta Cephei gave its name to the Cepheid variables that let astronomers measure the universe.
Contains the red hypergiant Mu Cephei, one of the largest stars known.
Cetus, the sea monster sent to devour Andromeda.
Mira, 'the wonderful', was the first variable star recognized — it brightens and fades over 11 months.
One of the largest constellations, sprawling across the equator.
The chameleon, a faint southern figure charted by Keyser and de Houtman.
Sits near the south celestial pole and never sets for southern polar observers.
The Chamaeleon dark clouds are a nearby nursery of newborn stars.
Pyxis, the mariner's compass, once part of the Ship Argo.
Contains T Pyxidis, a recurrent nova that erupts every few decades.
A faint equatorial constellation, best seen in southern winter.
Columba, carved out of Canis Major by Petrus Plancius in 1592.
Commemorates Noah's dove returning with the olive branch.
Contains the star Arneb, a supergiant at 2,600 light-years.
Coma Berenices honors Queen Berenice II, who cut off her hair as a temple offering.
Holds the Coma Cluster, thousands of galaxies whose orbits revealed dark matter.
The North Galactic Pole sits here — the least dusty window on the universe.
Corona Australis, the southern crown, a small arc of stars near the Teapot.
Contains the R Corona Australis reflection nebula, an active star nursery.
One of the smallest of the 88 constellations.
Corona Borealis, a perfect semicircle of stars often called 'the jewelry box'.
The Blaze Star, T Coronae Borealis, erupts as a nova roughly every 80 years.
Its brightest star, Alphecca, is an eclipsing binary with a dusty disk.
Corvus, the crow punished by Apollo for tardiness — its stars form a small kite.
Its four bright stars make it easy to spot despite its size.
The Antennae Galaxies, two colliding spirals, live here.
The goblet of Apollo, placed in the sky beside the crow and the water snake.
Once said to hold the wine of the gods.
A compact constellation of 4th-magnitude stars.
Crux, the Southern Cross — the smallest constellation of all 88, yet the southern sky's best-known landmark.
Appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Samoa and others.
The Coalsack, a nearby dark nebula, nestles beside its brightest stars.
Cygnus the Swan flies down the Milky Way along the Summer Triangle.
Deneb is one of the most luminous stars known — 160,000 times brighter than the Sun.
The Cygnus X-1 system was the first strong black-hole candidate ever identified.
Delphinus, a compact chevron of stars named by the Greeks after Poseidon's messenger.
Holds a nova that appeared in 1967, Nova Delphini 1967.
One of its stars, Rotanev, is named for an Italian astronomer's real name spelled backwards.
Dorado, the dolphinfish — Spanish explorers named it for the golden mahi-mahi.
Holds the Tarantula Nebula, the largest known stellar nursery in the Local Group.
The Large Magellanic Cloud dominates its patch of sky.
Draco coils between the Big and Little Dippers, guarding the pole in myth.
Thuban was the pole star when the Egyptians built the pyramids — it will be again someday.
The Cat's Eye Nebula here is one of the most complex planetary nebulae ever imaged.
Equuleus, the Little Horse, is the second-smallest constellation in the northern sky.
Has no stars brighter than 4th magnitude.
Charted by Ptolemy, yet almost nothing bright or famous lives here.
The celestial river, winding from Orion nearly to the south celestial pole.
Achernar, its southern star, is the flattest known star — spun so fast it bulges at the equator.
One of its regions hosts the 'Eridanus Supervoid', a vast cosmic cold spot.
Fornax, the laboratory furnace of Lacaille's instruments.
The Fornax Cluster is a rich gathering of galaxies, including the Great Barred Spiral.
Its deep-field images revealed hundreds of dwarf galaxies.
Castor and Pollux, the twin brothers of Greek myth, immortalized together.
Pollux hosts a confirmed planet; Castor is actually six stars bound in three pairs.
The Geminid meteor shower, one of the year's best, radiates from here.
Grus, the crane, formed from stars once part of the enormous Southern Fish.
Its brightest star, Alnair, means 'the bright one from the fish's tail'.
Home to a remarkable trio of interacting spiral galaxies.
The great hero of mythology, kneeling with his club raised.
Contains the Keystone asterism and the glorious M13 globular cluster.
M13 is the target of the 1974 Arecibo message — humanity's first deliberate broadcast to the stars.
Horologium, the pendulum clock, added by Lacaille to honor timekeeping.
Holds the Horologium Supercluster, tens of thousands of galaxies deep in the field.
A faint constellation far from the Milky Way's glare.
Hydra is the largest constellation of all 88, stretching a quarter of the way around the sky.
Its star Alphard means 'the solitary one' — the only bright star in that stretch of sky.
Home to the Ghost of Jupiter, a striking planetary nebula.
The Little Water Snake, distinct from the much larger Hydra.
Sits near the south celestial pole, wedged between the two Magellanic Clouds.
Charted by Dutch navigators around 1600.
Indus, the American Indian, honoring peoples encountered by European explorers.
Its brightest star is a close binary some 90 light-years away.
A dim southern constellation below the Peacock.
Lacerta, the lizard, squeezed into the sky by Hevelius between the Swan and the Ladder.
Holds the star BL Lacertae, prototype of a whole class of violently variable galaxies.
Contains the small open cluster NGC 7243.
Leo, the lion of Hercules's first labor, recognized by its backward-question-mark Sickle.
Regulus, the 'little king', sits almost exactly on the ecliptic.
The Leo Triplet of galaxies — M65, M66 and NGC 3628 — lies just under the Lion's hindquarters.
Leo Minor, the Lion Cub, carved from bare sky by Hevelius in 1687.
Its brightest star is an unusual, rapidly rotating giant.
Has no Messier objects and almost no bright deep-sky sights.
Lepus the Hare cowers beneath Orion's feet, chased by the Great Dog.
Contains Hind's Crimson Star, a deep-red carbon star famous for its color.
Globular cluster M79 lives here, unusually far from the galactic center.
Libra, the scales — once the claws of the Scorpion, later the only inanimate zodiac figure.
Its star names Zubeneschamali and Zubenelgenubi mean 'northern claw' and 'southern claw'.
The Sun's autumnal equinox point sits within its borders.
Lupus, the wolf, once visualized as an animal being carried to the altar of Centaurus.
Sits in a rich Milky Way region full of star clusters.
Contains the globular cluster NGC 5986.
A faint constellation Hevelius joked was named because you'd need lynx eyes to find anything in it.
Contains one of the oldest known star clusters, the 12-billion-year-old NGC 2419, the 'Intergalactic Wanderer'.
Its brightest star is a dazzling orange-red double.
Lyra holds Vega, once the pole star and due to be so again.
The Ring Nebula, M57, is one of the easiest planetary nebulae to see in small telescopes.
The mythic lyre of Orpheus, whose music charmed even stones.
The Table Mountain, named for the peak above Cape Town where Lacaille observed.
Contains part of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
The faintest constellation of the southern sky — no star brighter than 5th magnitude.
Microscopium, Lacaille's tribute to the microscope.
An obscure southern constellation with no bright stars.
Holds a galaxy cluster near the direction of the Great Attractor.
Monoceros the Unicorn, a young constellation first charted in 1613.
Contains the famous Rosette Nebula, a wreath of glowing gas.
Home to V838 Monocerotis, whose 2002 outburst lit up shells of dust in one of astronomy's great light echoes.
Musca the Fly, the only insect constellation, added by Dutch navigators.
Sits between the Southern Cross and the Chamaeleon.
Contains the eclipsing binary system Beta Muscae.
Norma, the carpenter's level, another Lacaille instrument.
Lies in the direction of the Milky Way's dense central bulge.
Holds open clusters and a pair of peculiar interacting galaxies.
Octans contains the south celestial pole — the southern counterpart of Polaris sits here.
Its pole star, Sigma Octantis, is barely visible to the naked eye.
Named after the octant, the forerunner of the sextant.
The Serpent Bearer, sometimes called the 13th zodiac figure — the Sun passes through it in December.
Contains Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in the sky.
Holds the dark nebula Barnard 68 and the recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi.
The Hunter, the most recognizable constellation in the sky — its three-belt asterism is famous worldwide.
The Orion Nebula is the nearest great stellar nursery, 1,300 light-years away.
Betelgeuse, a red supergiant, may one day explode as a supernova bright enough to see in daylight.
Pavo, the peacock — a constellation named for the showiest bird of them all.
Its brightest star, Alpha Pavonis, means simply 'the peacock'.
Contains NGC 6752, one of the best globular clusters for southern observers.
The winged horse of myth, whose Great Square anchors the autumn sky.
The star 51 Pegasi hosted the first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star.
Its hooves are said to create the spring of Hippocrene, source of poetic inspiration.
The hero who slew Medusa and rescued Andromeda.
Algol, the 'Demon Star', is a famous eclipsing binary that dims every 2.9 days.
The Perseid meteor shower, one of the year's finest, radiates from here every August.
The phoenix, the mythical bird reborn from its own ashes.
Contains the Phoenix Cluster, home to one of the most massive known galaxies.
Lies near the south celestial pole, best viewed from the Southern Hemisphere.
Pictor, the painter's easel, added by Lacaille.
Holds Beta Pictoris, famous for its debris disk — the first circumstellar disk imaged, in 1984.
Its stars are otherwise faint, making it a quiet patch of sky.
Pisces, the two fish of the zodiac, tied by a cord.
The March equinox point lies here now — the 'First Point of Aries' has drifted into the Fishes.
Contains M74, one of the most perfect spiral galaxies known.
Piscis Austrinus, the parent fish from which the two Pisces were said to spring.
Fomalhaut, its bright anchor, hosts the first directly imaged exoplanet orbiting a visible star.
Fomalhaut is sometimes called the Lonely Star of autumn — the only bright star in that region.
Puppis, the stern of the great ship Argo Navis.
Holds Puppis A, a supernova remnant 3,700 light-years away.
A rich Milky Way constellation with many open clusters.
Pyxis, the mariner's compass, once part of the Ship Argo.
Contains T Pyxidis, a recurrent nova that erupts every few decades.
A faint equatorial constellation, best seen in southern winter.
Reticulum, the reticle or grid at the eyepiece of a telescope.
Holds the interacting galaxy NGC 1559, home of a famous 2005 supernova.
One of Lacaille's smallest southern inventions.
Sagitta, the arrow — the third-smallest constellation of the 88.
Its brightest star, Sham, is an aging orange giant.
Contains the faint globular cluster M71 and the gorgeous Dumbbell's neighbor region.
Sagittarius, the archer, aims his arrow at the heart of the Milky Way.
The galactic center lies here — the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A* lives behind its stars.
The famous Teapot asterism sits within its borders.
Scorpius, the scorpion of Orion's fatal legend — the two constellations are placed on opposite sides of the sky.
Antares, its red supergiant heart, means 'rival of Mars'.
One of the most striking constellations, with a long curved tail of bright stars.
Sculptor, the sculptor's workshop, from Lacaille's era of tool constellations.
Contains the Sculptor Dwarf, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
The South Galactic Pole lies within its boundaries.
Scutum, the shield of John III Sobieski, King of Poland, added by Hevelius.
Holds the Wild Duck Cluster, M11, one of the richest open clusters known.
One of the smallest constellations, wedged between the Eagle and the Serpent.
Serpens is split in two by Ophiuchus — the only constellation divided into separate pieces.
Serpens Cauda (the tail) holds the Eagle Nebula and Pillars of Creation.
Serpens Caput (the head) contains the globular cluster M5.
Serpens is split in two by Ophiuchus — the only constellation divided into separate pieces.
Serpens Cauda (the tail) holds the Eagle Nebula and Pillars of Creation.
Serpens Caput (the head) contains the globular cluster M5.
Sextans, the sextant of navigation, another tool constellation.
Contains a distant galaxy cluster, Abell 2925.
Has no bright stars — its brightest is only 4th magnitude.
Taurus the Bull, with the V-shaped Hyades cluster forming its face.
Aldebaran, its orange eye, lies 65 light-years away.
The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, graze the Bull's shoulder — one of the most beautiful star clusters in the sky.
Telescopium, Lacaille's tribute to the telescope itself.
Contains the interacting group NGC 6845.
A faint southern constellation with few notable objects.
Triangulum, the triangle — one of Ptolemy's original 48 constellations.
Holds M33, the Triangulum Galaxy, third-largest member of the Local Group.
Represents the island of Sicily in one ancient tradition.
Triangulum Australe, the southern triangle, brighter and more compact than its northern cousin.
Its three stars form a nearly perfect equilateral triangle.
Contains the bright open cluster NGC 6025.
Tucana, the toucan of the southern sky, named by Dutch navigators.
Holds 47 Tucanae, the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky.
The Small Magellanic Cloud drifts within its borders.
Ursa Major, the Great Bear, whose Big Dipper asterism guides observers to the North Star.
M81 and M82, a famous interacting galaxy pair, live here.
Its Dipper stars move together as a genuine stellar family — the Ursa Major Moving Group.
Ursa Minor, the Little Bear, whose tail holds Polaris, the North Star.
Polaris lies almost exactly at the north celestial pole — it will drift away over centuries of precession.
The 'Little Dipper' has guided navigators for thousands of years.
Vela, the sails of the Argo, split off from the great ship in 1930.
Holds the Vela Pulsar, the remnant of a supernova seen about 11,000 years ago.
The Gum Nebula, one of the largest known emission nebulae, sprawls across its borders.
Virgo, the maiden of the zodiac — the second-largest constellation of the 88.
Spica, its brightest star, is actually four stars bound together.
The Virgo Cluster holds more than 1,300 galaxies — the nearest great cluster to our own.
Volans, the flying fish, named for the fish sailors saw gliding over the waves.
One of the smaller southern constellations, near the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Charted by Dutch navigators around 1600.
Vulpecula, the little fox, added by Hevelius in 1687.
Holds the Dumbbell Nebula, M27, one of the finest planetary nebulae for small telescopes.
Contains the famous Coathanger asterism, a hook of six stars easy to spot in binoculars.
